images.prompt: Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama. A small asteroid about the size of a clenched fist, built from tightly crumpled ivory card with a few graphite grit inclusions, hangs on a slim graphite rod stand above a pale neutral tabletop. Beneath it lies a flat ivory desk calendar with a blank grid of squares and crisp edges, and one square is marked by an acid-lime pin, the deadline. To the left, a small graphite desk lamp with a frosted acrylic shade lights the calendar; to the right, three graphite chairs stand pushed in neatly. The asteroid's creases hold faint dust, and a single crumb of card has fallen onto the calendar, the only hint of what is coming. Wide 16:9 landscape frame. The hero object sits slightly left of centre on the lower third, with the related objects extending to the right so the workflow reads left to right. Clean, generous negative space above. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: one large soft key light from the upper left at about 45 degrees, like diffused north-window daylight, with a gentle white bounce fill from the right; soft grounded contact shadows fall to the lower right. Camera: 100mm macro lens at f/4, eye level with the tabletop, three-quarter view. The hero object is tack sharp and the background melts into smooth, creamy blur on a seamless pale neutral sweep. Mood: calm, precise, orderly and quietly premium, like high-end editorial product photography. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes. No readable text, letters, numbers, clock digits, logos, signage or user-interface graphics anywhere. No holograms, floating screens, robots with faces, dense cable tangles, carnival or circus elements, cartoon or plastic CGI look, oversaturated colour, lens flare or heavy vignette.

Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama, captured mid-disaster. The asteroid has swelled as the deadline closed in, now as wide as the desk and pressing down on the same calendar, whose pages have split and folded under it. Its graphite rod stand has bent in a shallow arc. Small graphite drills are embedded in its surface at several angles, left running by the desk team, and one is frozen mid-slip out of its bore with a spray of card crumbs. The acid-lime pin has been pushed up through a torn calendar square and is tilting toward the edge. The chairs have been shoved back and one has tipped over, a jacket crumpled beneath it. Card grit and dust drift down from the drill holes onto the lamp shade. Wide 16:9 landscape frame, same layout and angle as the calm version of this scene. The hero object stays slightly left of centre, and the spread of the disaster runs to the right and toward the camera so its path can be traced back to the source. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: the same soft upper-left key and right-side bounce fill as a calm studio setup, unchanged, so the disorder reads as physical and real rather than theatrical. Airborne paper, grains and fragments catch the key light with crisp edge highlights. Camera: 85mm lens at f/5.6, same three-quarter tabletop angle, fast shutter freezing everything mid-air. Focus sits where the chain reaction started, and the spread softens into the depth of field. Mood: absurd but plausible, an orderly system that got out of hand, still clean and editorial. Photorealistic photograph of a vast handcrafted miniature landscape diorama. A cratered field of pale compacted card dust stretches to a curved, hazy horizon, its surface pocked with shallow impact bowls rimmed with debris. In the largest crater lies the asteroid, now as big as a hill, cracked across its middle and bristling with old graphite drills snapped off at their bases. The desk calendar is a set of broken ivory slabs radiating out from under it, and the lamp stands on the crater rim, its frosted shade split. A slim graphite drill rig with a lime bit has cut the asteroid cleanly in half along the crack, and a narrow conveyor beside it is stacking the cut blocks into a level plinth where a new blank calendar sheet has been laid. Wide 16:9 panoramic frame. The main ruin anchors the left or centre foreground, terrain rolls back to a distant horizon on the upper third, and the lime recovery rig sits in the right midground. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: soft overcast late-afternoon daylight still falling from the upper left, with long soft shadows grounding the ruins and atmospheric haze fading distant forms into pale grey-green.
